16nav8p:234: A widely overlooked issue in enterprise AI transformation: the prettier the front-end AI application, the heavier the unstructured data governance debt at the back end. Zhang Sensen uses a precise metaphor to describe this phenomenon—"the front end is beautiful, the back end is drenched in rain." The automotive industry case shows: when leadership demands "AI ASAP," teams with weak data and governance foundations can only choose the easiest path to visible results (such as AI Coding), while the real data governance work gets postponed, causing technical debt to accumulate continuously. This "showcase project → technical debt accumulation → increased system fragility" pattern is harder to repay than traditional software engineering technical debt, because it faces large volumes of uncontrollable unstructured data.
172uvac:333: The team practice of Ma Jinlong (Qiming Zhiyuan), spun off from the parent company, provides a real case of building an AI Native organization from scratch. Three key insights: (1) information must primarily be AI-readable—all documents must be in Markdown format, with PDF/Word strictly prohibited; AI is the main force, humans are assistants (a fundamental shift in role perception); (2) domains such as finance and legal that cannot be AI-ified are explicitly handled by humans, and AI Native is not forced; (3) stay open to current judgments—model capability changes 6–18 months later may overturn today's architectural assumptions. At the practical level: the team no longer distinguishes between front-end, back-end, testing, and algorithm roles; "one person becomes a hexahedron with the help of AI capabilities," AI covers 70–80% of the work, and humans do judgment and checks. The greatest difficulty has instead become "finding the right problems"—"there is no shortage of solutions now; what is lacking is problems, what is lacking is pain points."

1eynvkt:263: The historical analogy proposed by Zheng Yan (Huawei) is highly insightful: factories in the steam engine era placed a large steam engine at the center of the workshop, driving all machines through a main shaft and belts. When electrification arrived, British factories simply replaced the steam engine with an electric motor, changing nothing else. The true production revolution—the assembly line—was realized by Ford in America. This analogy precisely illustrates: merely layering AI technology onto old organizational structures ("swapping the engine") without redesigning business processes and organizational structures cannot achieve true AI transformation. "If you really want to transform, perhaps you truly need to start from a very small company state"—this explains why large enterprises' AI transformations always make "more thunder than rain," while startups find it easier to achieve AI-Native organizational forms.

The result is that enterprises view AI as a cost-cutting tool (layoffs) rather than an opportunity for process reinvention.
